The Story of Marichi

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who is like a cloud that makes the paddy of happiness grow green, and I write the story of Marichi, son of Bharat, as found in the scriptures.

In Ayodhya, Emperor Bharat, lord of the world, had a son named Marichi. Marichi was worthy of liberation and simple-hearted. When Lord Adinath, who is always worshipped by Indra, Dharanendra, the Vidyadharas, Chakravartins, and all great beings, renounced the world and became a monk, four thousand kings also became monks along with him. Marichi, the hero of this story, was among those monks.

One day King Bharat went to the Samavasaran to hear Lord Adinath's discourse. After bowing to the Lord, he asked, "Bhagavan, I have learned from your teaching that after you there will be twenty-three more Tirthankaras. But is there anyone in this assembly who is destined to become a Tirthankara?" The Lord replied, "Yes, there is. That is your son Marichi, who will be famous as the last Tirthankara, Mahavir. There is no doubt about this."

Hearing this, Bharat's joy knew no bounds. But from that very moment, Marichi's mind turned perverse. Pride arose in him: "Since I am destined to become a Tirthankara anyway, why should I endure the hardships of nakedness, suffering, and restricted food? Why not live comfortably in some other guise?" As soon as these thoughts arose, he abandoned all vows, restraints, conduct, and right faith. He became an ascetic of his own invention, creating several false doctrines based on Samkhya and other philosophies, and thus became the cause of his own terrible suffering in the world.

After that, he wandered through many lower births. Truly, negligence, carelessness, and passions are great obstacles on the path of welfare for living beings. Even those worthy of liberation, through ignorance, become negligent and suffer. Therefore, the wise should never be negligent in religious duties.

Through the play of delusion, Marichi had to wander in the world for a long time. Later, when some of his sinful karma subsided, he again found the path of Jain dharma. Through its grace, he became a king named Nand. Then, for some reason, he became detached from the world. As a monk, he bound the karma that determines the name of a Tirthankara through sixteen types of contemplation. From there he went to heaven. After his heavenly lifespan was complete, he was born as the son of King Priyamitra and Queen Priyamkara in the city of Kundalpur. He was named Marichi again. Through intense austerity and meditation, he destroyed his karmas and became the twenty-fourth and last Tirthankara — Lord Mahavir.

This story teaches that destiny alone is not enough. Even though Marichi was destined to become a Tirthankara, his pride and negligence caused him to wander through countless births before fulfilling that destiny. The wise should not rely on destiny but should practise dharma with diligence and humility.
